definition: Memory on a thread's call stack, where each active function call keeps its frame. Allocating it means moving the stack pointer, so it is almost free, but nothing stored there can outlive the call that created it.
example: On Linux the main thread's stack is commonly limited to 8 MiB; `ulimit -s` shows the limit.

definition: A large pool of memory from which blocks can be allocated and freed in any order. It holds values that must outlive the function that made them, whose size is only known at run time, that are large, or that are shared. It has nothing to do with the heap data structure.
example: A Python list, a Java object created with `new` and a Rust `Box` all live in heap memory.

definition: The stretch of a program's run during which a value exists and may be used, from its creation to its destruction. Memory management is mostly about deciding when each lifetime ends and making sure nothing uses the value afterwards.
example: A C local variable's lifetime ends when its function returns; a value stored in a global lives until the program exits.

definition: A CPU register that holds the address of the current top of the call stack. Allocating a frame moves it by the frame's size (downwards on x86 and ARM), and returning moves it back.
example: On x86-64 the stack pointer is the RSP register.

definition: The address of the instruction to continue from when a function finishes, saved (usually in the stack frame or a link register) when the function is called.

The few instructions a compiler places at the start of a function to set up its stack frame, such as moving the stack pointer and saving registers. The matching epilogue undoes them before the function returns.

The rule that the stack pointer, or a value in memory, must sit at an address that is a multiple of a fixed number of bytes. Compilers pad frames to keep it, because misaligned access is slower or not allowed on some processors.
example: The x86-64 System V convention requires the stack to be 16-byte aligned at each function call.

definition: A list an allocator keeps of the blocks of memory that are currently free. Allocating means searching it for a block big enough; freeing puts a block back on it.
example: After a 64-byte block is freed, a typical allocator puts it on its 64-byte free list and may hand it straight to the next 64-byte request.

definition: An allocation method where free memory is one contiguous region and a pointer marks where it starts. Allocating n bytes returns the current pointer and advances it by n, which takes only a few instructions; it works when compaction, copying or whole-region freeing keeps the free space contiguous.
example: With the pointer at address 1,000, a 48-byte request returns 1,000 and moves the pointer to 1,048.

definition: The library code (or runtime component) that hands out blocks of heap memory on request and takes them back when they are freed, keeping track of which parts of the heap are in use.
example: glibc's malloc, jemalloc and Go's runtime allocator are all memory allocators.

definition: The C standard library function that allocates a block of at least the requested number of bytes on the heap and returns a pointer to it, or NULL if it fails. The block's contents are not initialised, and it must later be released with free.
example: `malloc(10 * sizeof(int))` asks for room for 10 ints, usually 40 bytes.

definition: The C function that returns a block obtained from malloc, calloc or realloc to the allocator. free(NULL) does nothing; freeing the same block twice, or using it after freeing, is undefined behaviour.
The C function that allocates heap memory for an array of a given number of elements of a given size and fills it with zero bytes.
example: `calloc(100, sizeof(int))` returns room for 100 ints, all set to 0.

definition: The C function that resizes a heap block, possibly by moving it to a new address and freeing the old one. On success the old pointer must no longer be used; on failure for a nonzero size the original block is left untouched.

The C standard's term for how long an object's storage lasts: automatic (until its block ends, typically a stack frame or a register), static (the whole program run), thread (the thread's run) or allocated (from malloc until free).
example: `int x;` inside a function has automatic storage duration; `static int n;` has static storage duration.

definition: A variable whose storage lasts for the whole program run, such as a C global, a C local declared static, or a Java static field. In garbage-collected languages, static and global variables are GC roots, so whatever they point to stays alive.
example: A Java `static Map` used as a cache keeps every entry reachable until the entry is removed.

definition: A pointer value that deliberately points at nothing, written NULL in C (nullptr in C++). Allocation functions return it on failure; dereferencing it is undefined behaviour, though on common systems it usually crashes.
example: `malloc` returns NULL when it cannot allocate the requested memory.

definition: A C, C++ and Objective-C compiler from the LLVM project, widely used on macOS, Linux and in Chromium. It includes AddressSanitizer and many warnings about memory bugs.
example: Clang warns 'address of stack memory associated with local variable returned' for the classic dangling-pointer bug.

definition: The GNU Compiler Collection: the long-standing open-source compiler for C, C++ and other languages, the default on most Linux distributions. Like Clang it supports AddressSanitizer through -fsanitize=address.

A compiler analysis that works out whether a value, or a pointer to it, can still be reached after the function that created it returns (whether it 'escapes'). Values that don't escape can stay on the stack or be removed entirely; escaping ones need heap storage.
example: Go's compiler reports `moved to heap: p` when a function returns `&p`.

definition: HotSpot's optimising JIT compiler, used for frequently executed ('hot') code. Among many optimisations it performs escape analysis and can remove allocations of objects that never escape.
A JIT optimisation that, once escape analysis proves an object never leaves a method, removes the object's allocation and keeps its fields as separate local variables or registers instead.
example: A `Point` created and used only inside a hot loop can become two plain ints, x and y, with no heap allocation.

definition: A Go compiler flag (used as `go build -gcflags=-m`) that prints the compiler's optimisation decisions, including which values escape to the heap and which functions are inlined.
example: Its output contains lines such as `moved to heap: p` and `x does not escape`.

definition: In Go, a value of an interface type, stored as two words: one pointing at type information and one pointing at (or holding) the concrete value. Storing a value in an interface can make it escape to the heap.
Rust's owned, growable UTF-8 text type. Like Vec, it is a pointer, length and capacity, with the characters in a heap buffer it owns; assigning it moves ownership rather than copying the text.
example: `String::from("hi")` allocates a 2-byte buffer for the text.

definition: Rust's unsigned integer type that is as wide as a pointer: 64 bits (8 bytes) on 64-bit targets. It is used for lengths, capacities and indices.

A lightweight thread managed by the Go runtime rather than the operating system. Each starts with a small stack (a few kilobytes) that the runtime grows by copying it to a bigger one, so a program can run hundreds of thousands of them.
example: `go handle(conn)` starts a new goroutine.

definition: A thread created and scheduled by the operating system kernel. Each has its own fixed-maximum stack, typically reserved at around 1 to 8 MiB, which is why programs cannot create hundreds of thousands of them the way Go creates goroutines.
example: A Java platform thread is a thin wrapper around one OS thread.

definition: A Unix shell command that shows or sets per-process resource limits. `ulimit -s` shows the main thread's stack size limit in kibibytes.
example: On many Linux systems `ulimit -s` prints 8192, meaning 8 MiB.

definition: The HotSpot JVM option that sets the stack size of each Java thread.
example: `java -Xss2m App` gives each thread a 2 MiB stack.

definition: The error that occurs when a thread's call stack grows past its maximum size, usually because of very deep or unbounded recursion or very large local variables. C programs typically crash with a segmentation fault; Java throws StackOverflowError.
A page of memory deliberately left inaccessible next to a stack (or other region). Touching it triggers a fault, so a stack overflow crashes cleanly instead of silently overwriting other memory.
The basic unit of memory: 8 bits on all modern computers, and the smallest piece of memory with its own address. Sizes of objects, buffers and heaps are counted in bytes.
example: An i32 takes 4 bytes; a pointer on a 64-bit machine takes 8.

definition: Kilobyte: 1,000 bytes in the SI (decimal) sense, although it is sometimes used loosely for 1,024 bytes (properly a kibibyte, KiB).
Kibibyte: 1,024 (2^10) bytes, the binary counterpart of the kilobyte.
example: A 2 KiB goroutine stack is 2,048 bytes.

definition: Megabyte: 1,000,000 bytes in the SI (decimal) sense; sometimes used loosely for 1,048,576 bytes (properly a mebibyte, MiB).
Mebibyte: 1,048,576 (2^20) bytes, the binary counterpart of the megabyte. Stack sizes and memory limits are often given in MiB.
example: 8 MiB is 8,388,608 bytes.

definition: Gigabyte: 1,000,000,000 bytes in the SI (decimal) sense; sometimes used loosely for 2^30 bytes (properly a gibibyte, GiB).
Gibibyte: 1,073,741,824 (2^30) bytes, or 1,024 MiB, the binary counterpart of the gigabyte.
example: A 2 GiB container limit is 2,048 MiB.

definition: Describes a processor and operating system whose registers and memory addresses are 64 bits (8 bytes) wide, as on x86-64 and ARM64. Pointers on such systems take 8 bytes.
A family of processor instruction sets used in almost all phones and in many laptops and servers; AArch64 (ARM64) is its 64-bit version.
Variable-length array: a C array declared with a size known only at run time, such as `int a[n];`, typically placed on the stack. Introduced in C99 and made optional in C11.
A language behaviour where assigning or passing a value copies the data, so the two variables are independent afterwards.
example: Assigning one C struct to another copies all its fields.

definition: A language behaviour where assigning or passing a value copies only a reference to it, so both names refer to the same object and changes through one are seen through the other.
example: In Python, `b = a` makes b refer to the same list as a.

definition: A Rust marker trait for types that can be duplicated by simply copying their bits, such as integers, floats, bool, char, and tuples or arrays of them. Assigning a Copy value copies it and leaves the original usable instead of moving it.
example: `let y = x;` with an i32 x leaves both x and y usable.

definition: In CPython 3.12 and later, an object such as None, True or a small integer whose reference count is pinned so that ordinary increments and decrements never free it (PEP 683). This avoids writes to objects shared between threads or processes and helps multi-threaded and multi-process use.
An object of which only one instance exists and is shared by everything that uses it.
example: In Python, every `None` in a program is the same object.

definition: A build of CPython with the GIL removed, so Python threads can run in parallel: experimental in 3.13 and officially supported (though still optional) from 3.14 (PEP 779). It uses biased reference counting and other changes to keep reference counts correct across threads (PEP 703).
Global interpreter lock: the lock in standard CPython that lets only one thread execute Python bytecode at a time. It made plain, non-atomic reference-count updates safe.
The Python Enhancement Proposal that introduced immortal objects in Python 3.12: objects whose reference counts never reach zero, so they are never freed and their counts need not be written.
The Python Enhancement Proposal for making the global interpreter lock optional, which led to the free-threaded CPython build and its biased reference counting.
The Python Enhancement Proposal (Python 3.4) for safe object finalisation, which lets the cycle collector free cycles containing objects with __del__ methods instead of leaving them in gc.garbage.
A loop or code path that runs so often that it dominates a program's running time, so small costs inside it, such as a heap allocation per iteration, add up.
The short, common-case route through some code, kept as cheap as possible; the rare, more expensive cases are handled by a separate slow path.
example: A bump allocator's fast path is 'advance the pointer'; its slow path asks for a new chunk of memory.

definition: A language runtime (such as the JVM, .NET, the Go runtime or CPython) that manages memory for the program, usually with a garbage collector, so the programmer never calls free.
A program that executes another program's code directly, statement by statement or bytecode by bytecode, rather than compiling it to machine code first. CPython is an interpreter.
The natural unit of data for a processor: as wide as its registers and pointers, 8 bytes on a 64-bit machine.
example: A Rust Vec header is three machine words: 24 bytes on a 64-bit target.

definition: The range of memory addresses a process can use. Each process has its own, and the operating system reclaims all of it when the process exits.
The fixed-size unit (commonly 4 KiB) in which the operating system maps, shares and copies memory.
example: After fork, parent and child share each page until one of them writes to it.

definition: A running program with its own address space and resources, managed by the operating system. Memory a process allocates is returned to the system when it exits.

A bug where a program reads or writes a heap block after freeing it, through a dangling pointer. The allocator may already have given the memory to something else, so the bug causes corruption and is a common route to exploitation.
example: Calling `free(u)` and then reading `u->name` is a use-after-free.

definition: A bug where the same heap block is freed twice. It is undefined behaviour and can corrupt the allocator's bookkeeping, which attackers can sometimes exploit.
A bug where a program writes past the end (or before the start) of a block of memory, overwriting neighbouring data or allocator metadata. An off-by-one overflow writes just one byte too many.
example: Copying a 2-character string plus its NUL into a 2-byte block writes 1 byte past the end.

definition: Reading memory before anything has been written to it. In C its contents are indeterminate (often stale data from an earlier use), so the program may behave unpredictably or leak secrets.
Memory a garbage-collected program keeps reachable but will never use again, such as entries in a cache that is never evicted. The collector cannot free it, because it only frees unreachable memory.
example: A global dictionary that gains an entry per request and never loses one is a logical leak.

definition: The idea that each piece of memory has an owner responsible for freeing it. In C it is only a convention recorded in documentation; C++ expresses it with smart pointers; Rust's compiler enforces it, with exactly one owner per value.
example: A C function documented 'caller owns result' expects you to free what it returns.

definition: An arrangement where several owners keep one object alive, usually by reference counting, so it is freed only when the last owner lets go.
example: C++ `std::shared_ptr` and Rust `Rc<T>` provide shared ownership.

definition: Out of memory. On Linux, when memory runs out (or a container exceeds its memory limit) the kernel's OOM killer terminates a process to free memory; this is an OOM kill.
example: A Go service in a 2 GiB container is OOM-killed if its memory use exceeds 2 GiB.

definition: An attacker's ability to make a program run code of the attacker's choosing, the most serious outcome of a memory-safety bug.
Defences that check, at run time, that indirect calls and returns go only to legitimate targets, making it harder to turn memory corruption into code execution.
A basic capability an attacker gains from a bug, such as writing chosen bytes to a chosen address, which can be combined into a full exploit.

The guarantee that a program cannot read or write memory it does not own: no dangling pointers, no out-of-bounds access, no double frees. Java, Go, Python, C#, Swift and safe Rust provide it; C and C++ do not.
A run-time check that an array index lies inside the array before it is used, so an out-of-bounds access raises an error instead of touching other memory.
example: In Java, `a[10]` on a 10-element array throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.

definition: Foreign function interface: a mechanism for calling code written in another language, usually C. Memory crossing an FFI boundary is outside the calling language's safety guarantees.
example: Rust calls C libraries through FFI; Go uses cgo.

definition: A C pattern where every error path jumps (with goto) to one cleanup block at the end of the function that releases everything acquired so far, so nothing is leaked or freed twice.
example: The Linux kernel uses `goto out;` labels for this throughout.

definition: Allocating many objects that share one lifetime from a large block (an arena or region), usually by bumping a pointer, and then freeing the whole arena at once instead of object by object.
example: A compiler can allocate every syntax-tree node for one pass from an arena and free it in one call when the pass ends.

definition: A widely used open-source web server and reverse proxy, written in C, which allocates per-request memory from pools freed when the request finishes.

Resource acquisition is initialisation: the C++ technique of tying a resource (memory, a file, a lock) to an object, so the object's destructor releases it automatically when the object goes out of scope, including during exception unwinding.
example: A `std::lock_guard` unlocks its mutex when the enclosing block ends.

definition: A special function that runs when an object's lifetime ends, used to release what the object owns. In C++ it is written ~ClassName; Rust's equivalent is the drop method of the Drop trait.
example: `~unique_ptr()` deletes the object the pointer owns.

definition: The C++ smart pointer that is the single owner of a heap object: it cannot be copied, only moved, and deletes the object in its destructor. std::make_unique creates one.
example: `auto p = std::make_unique<Widget>();` frees the Widget when p goes out of scope.

definition: The C++ smart pointer for shared ownership: copies share a reference count (in a separate control block), and the object is deleted when the last shared_ptr to it is destroyed. Its count updates are atomic.
The C++ weak reference that goes with shared_ptr: it watches an object without keeping it alive. lock() returns a shared_ptr if the object still exists, or an empty one if not.
The separate heap allocation that std::shared_ptr uses to hold an object's strong and weak reference counts (and its deleter).
example: std::make_shared usually puts the object and its control block in one allocation.

definition: The function or object a C++ smart pointer calls to destroy what it owns; by default it calls delete.
What happens when an exception propagates: the runtime leaves each abandoned function in turn and, in C++ and Rust, runs the destructors of its local objects on the way.

A C++ standard function that casts an object so that a move constructor or move assignment can take its resources. It does not move anything by itself; the moved-from object stays valid but usually empty.
example: After `auto q = std::move(p);` a unique_ptr p is null.

definition: Transferring a value's resources (such as a heap buffer) to a new owner instead of copying them. In Rust a move invalidates the source variable at compile time; in C++ the moved-from object remains usable but in a valid, typically empty, state.
example: `let s2 = s1;` moves a Rust String: only s2 owns the buffer afterwards.

definition: Whether an object can be got to by following references from the GC roots (stacks, registers, globals). Garbage collectors free unreachable objects; reachable ones stay, whether or not the program will use them again.
example: Two objects that point only at each other, with no path from a root, are unreachable.

definition: Go's typed pipe for sending values between goroutines. A goroutine waiting to receive from a channel nobody sends on is blocked forever, and everything its stack references stays alive.
A Java statement that opens resources in its header and closes them automatically when the block exits, normally or by exception.
example: `try (var in = new FileInputStream(f)) { ... }` closes the file at the end of the block.

definition: A Go statement that schedules a function call to run when the surrounding function returns, commonly used to close files or unlock mutexes on every exit path.
Rust's destructor mechanism: a type implementing Drop has its drop method run automatically when a value of it goes out of scope. Rust calls this 'dropping' the value.
example: A MutexGuard's Drop unlocks the mutex.

definition: A memory-error detector built into Clang and GCC (enable with -fsanitize=address). The compiler adds checks around memory accesses, so heap-use-after-free, buffer overflows and double frees are reported with stack traces. Typical slowdown is about 2x.
Extra checking or recording code inserted into a program, by the compiler or at run time, to observe its behaviour.
In AddressSanitizer, poisoned bytes placed around each allocation; any access to them is reported as an overflow.

A tool suite that runs an unmodified program on a simulated CPU; its default tool, Memcheck, checks every memory access for errors. No recompilation is needed, but programs run roughly 20 to 30 times slower.
A memory-leak detector built into Clang and GCC, enabled by default with AddressSanitizer on Linux, that reports allocations still unreachable when the program exits.
A compiler-inserted run-time checker for one class of bugs, such as AddressSanitizer (memory errors), LeakSanitizer (leaks) or ThreadSanitizer (data races).
Automatically generating huge numbers of unusual or malformed inputs to find ones that crash a program. Combined with sanitizers it finds many memory-safety bugs.
A coverage-guided fuzzer from the LLVM project that runs inside the process under test and is usually combined with AddressSanitizer.
American Fuzzy Lop: a widely used coverage-guided fuzzer, now maintained as AFL++.
The open-source browser project behind Google Chrome and several other browsers, written mostly in C++.
A security bug that reveals data an attacker should not see, such as stale memory contents or addresses.
The C function that returns the length of a NUL-terminated string in bytes, not counting the terminating NUL.
example: `strlen("hi")` is 2, but the string occupies 3 bytes.

definition: The C function that copies a NUL-terminated string, including its NUL, into a destination buffer without checking the buffer's size.
A C function that allocates a new heap copy of a string with malloc and returns it; the caller must free it. Standard since C23 and long available in POSIX.
The C function that returns a pointer to the value of an environment variable. The string belongs to the environment, so the caller must not free it.
The C function that formats text into a buffer, writing at most the given number of bytes including the terminating NUL.
The C functions that open a file and return a FILE pointer (fopen), and close it again (fclose). Like memory, every opened file must be closed exactly once.
The C function that ends the process immediately and abnormally, without running normal cleanup such as C++ destructors of live objects.
The character with code 0, written '\0'. C marks the end of every string with one, so a string of n characters needs n + 1 bytes.
example: "hi" is stored as the 3 bytes h, i, \0.

definition: A sequence of characters stored as bytes and ended by a NUL byte, with no separate length; functions like strlen find the end by scanning for the NUL.
The end of a process's run. The operating system then reclaims its whole address space, so memory leaked by a short-lived program is returned anyway.

The number stored with an object that records how many strong references currently point at it. Reference counting adds one when a reference is created, subtracts one when one is destroyed, and frees the object when the count reaches zero.
example: After `a = Obj(); b = a` the object's reference count is 2.

definition: An ordinary reference that keeps its target alive: it counts towards the reference count and is followed by a tracing collector.

A reference that points at an object without keeping it alive: it does not count towards the reference count. When the object is freed, the weak reference becomes empty instead of dangling. Used to break reference cycles.
example: A tree node's pointer to its parent is usually a weak reference.

definition: Rust's weak reference for Rc and Arc. It does not keep the value alive; upgrade() returns Some(strong reference) if the value still exists, or None if it has been dropped.

Rust's single-threaded reference-counted pointer: several Rc handles share ownership of one heap value, which is dropped when the last handle goes. Its count updates are plain (non-atomic), so the compiler forbids sending it to another thread.
example: `let a = Rc::clone(&cfg);` makes a second owner of the same value.

definition: Rust's atomically reference-counted pointer: like Rc but with atomic count updates, so it can be shared between threads. It does not by itself make the inner value safe to mutate; that needs a Mutex or similar.

Automatic Reference Counting: the memory management used by Swift and Objective-C, in which the compiler inserts retain and release (increment and decrement) operations. It has no cycle collector, so cycles must be broken with weak or unowned references.
Swift and Objective-C's names for incrementing (retain) and decrementing (release) an object's reference count. The Swift optimiser removes pairs it can prove cancel out.

A Swift reference that does not keep its target alive, like a weak one, but is not optional: you promise the target outlives it. Accessing a deallocated target through a checked unowned reference traps; unowned(unsafe) removes that check.
In Swift, a list at the start of a closure saying how it captures outside values, such as [weak self] to capture self weakly and avoid a reference cycle.
example: `{ [weak self] in self?.count += 1 }`

definition: In Apple's UIKit, an object that manages one screen (or part of one) of an app's user interface.

A method a runtime calls on an object just before reclaiming it, such as Python's __del__. Unlike a C++ destructor, its timing is not guaranteed under tracing GC, so it should not be relied on to close files.
When a finalizer stores a reference to its dying object somewhere reachable, bringing it back to life, so the runtime must not free it after all.

A memory operation, such as an increment, that other threads see as happening all at once, never half-done. Atomic increments keep shared reference counts correct across threads but cost more than plain ones, especially under contention.
example: Two threads doing a plain `count += 1` at the same moment can lose one update; an atomic increment cannot.

definition: The rules about the order in which one thread's memory writes become visible to other threads. Stronger orderings are safer but make atomic operations slower.

A reference-counting scheme in which the thread that owns an object updates a fast, non-atomic local count, while other threads update a separate atomic shared count. Free-threaded CPython uses it (PEP 703).

The chain reaction when freeing one reference-counted object drops the counts of everything it refers to to zero, which frees them in turn, and so on. Releasing a huge structure this way can take a long time all at once.
example: Dropping the last reference to a 10-million-node tree frees all 10 million nodes on the spot.

definition: A technique where two processes (or values) share the same memory until one writes to it, at which point only the written page is copied. After fork, parent and child share all pages this way.
The Unix system call that creates a new process as a copy of the calling one. Memory is shared copy-on-write, so pages are only copied when either process writes to them.

Python's interface to CPython's cycle collector: gc.collect() runs a collection now, gc.disable() and gc.enable() switch automatic collection off and on, gc.freeze() moves existing objects to a permanent generation it ignores, and gc.set_threshold() tunes how often it runs.

A collector that runs alongside reference counting to find and free groups of objects that refer to each other but are unreachable from outside, which counting alone can never free. CPython's lives in the gc module.

A loop of references in which objects (directly or indirectly) refer back to themselves, such as a parent and child pointing at each other. Under pure reference counting every count in the loop stays above zero, so an unreachable cycle is never freed.
example: A doubly linked list is full of reference cycles.

definition: In CPython, an object that can hold references to other objects, such as a list, dict or class instance. Only containers can take part in reference cycles, so they are the only objects the cycle collector tracks.

A garbage-collection design that splits objects by age and collects the young ones much more often than the old ones, because most objects die young. Pointers from old objects to young ones are tracked with a write barrier.
example: The JVM's G1 and CPython's cycle collector are both generational.

definition: A reference-counting optimisation that skips count updates for references held in local variables and on the stack, and reconciles them periodically by scanning the stacks, trading slightly delayed freeing for much less count traffic.
Apple's development environment for macOS and iOS. Its memory graph debugger shows objects and the references between them, which helps find retain cycles.
A linked list in which each node points to both the next and the previous node, so every pair of neighbours forms a reference cycle.

Garbage collection that finds live objects by following references from the GC roots and frees everything it did not reach. Unreachable cycles are freed naturally. Java, Go, C# and JavaScript engines use it.

A reference the running program can use without following any other pointer: local variables in thread stacks, CPU registers, global and static variables, and some runtime internals. A tracing collector starts from the roots; anything it cannot reach from them is garbage.
example: A local variable holding a list in a running function is a root, so the list stays alive.

definition: An object a garbage collector must keep because it is reachable from the roots. 'Live data' or the 'live heap' means the total size of such objects; it sets the minimum cost of tracing and the minimum heap size.
example: A service with 2 GB of live data needs a heap of more than 2 GB, usually much more.

definition: Java Native Interface: the JVM's mechanism for calling C or C++ code and letting it hold references to Java objects. References handed to native code are treated as GC roots.

The original tracing collector design: a mark phase walks the object graph from the roots and marks every object it reaches, then a sweep phase walks the whole heap and frees every unmarked object. Objects are never moved, so free space becomes fragmented.
A flag on (or alongside) each heap object that the collector sets when it reaches the object during marking; unmarked objects are garbage.
The work list of objects a collector has reached but not yet scanned, kept as an explicit data structure rather than by recursion, so a long chain of objects cannot overflow the native stack.
The network formed by heap objects (as nodes) and the references between them (as edges). Tracing collectors walk it from the roots.
The state where free heap memory is split into many small, scattered holes between live objects, so a large allocation can fail, or need a slow search, even though plenty of memory is free in total.
example: Three free 1 KB holes cannot satisfy one 2 KB request.

definition: A tracing collector that marks live objects and then slides them together so all free space forms one contiguous block, removing fragmentation and allowing bump-pointer allocation, at the cost of extra passes to compute new addresses and fix every pointer.
example: HotSpot's Serial and Parallel collectors compact the old generation this way.

definition: A tracing collector that splits memory into two halves and, when the active half fills, copies every reachable object into the other half and abandons the first. Its work is proportional to live data only and it never fragments, but it needs twice the space and moves objects.
example: If 2% of a 100 MB half-space is live, a collection copies about 2 MB.

definition: In a copying collector, the half of memory the program has been allocating into; at collection time live objects are copied out of it and the rest is discarded.
In a copying collector, the empty half of memory that live objects are copied into during a collection; afterwards the two halves swap roles.
An address left in the old copy of an object that a collector has moved, pointing at the new copy, so that other references to the old copy can be redirected and the object is copied only once.
C. J. Cheney's 1970 copying-collection algorithm, which copies live objects breadth-first using just a scan pointer and a free pointer into to-space instead of a stack or recursion.
Visiting a graph level by level: everything one step from the start, then everything two steps away, and so on, using a queue.
Visiting a graph by following each path as far as it goes before backing up to try the next, using a stack or recursion.
A collector that knows exactly which words in objects, stacks and registers are pointers, from type information and compiler-generated stack maps. Only a precise collector can safely move any object.
example: The JVM and Go collectors are precise.

definition: A collector that treats any word that looks like a heap address as a possible pointer, because it lacks exact type information. It can work with C and C++ without compiler help, but may keep garbage alive and cannot move objects referenced by ambiguous words.
The Boehm-Demers-Weiser collector: a widely used conservative, non-moving garbage collector that can be linked into C and C++ programs as a replacement for malloc and free.
A table produced by the compiler that records, for particular points in the code (safepoints), which stack slots and registers hold pointers, so a precise collector can find and update them.
A hybrid collector that pins (does not move) objects referenced from ambiguous roots such as the C stack, and copies all the others.

The empirical observation that, in many programs, most objects become unreachable soon after they are created, while a minority live a long time. Generational collectors are built on it; it holds for many workloads but not all.
The part of a generational heap where new objects are allocated. It is collected often and quickly, because most of its objects are already dead; survivors are copied out.
The part of a generational heap holding objects that have survived several young collections. It is collected less often, and its collections are usually more expensive.
In HotSpot's generational collectors, the area of the young generation where new objects are first allocated.
In HotSpot's generational collectors, one of the young-generation areas that holds objects which survived a minor collection but are not yet old enough to promote.

A collection of only the young generation. It is usually fast because it copies only the few survivors, treating references from old objects (found through the card table or remembered sets) as extra roots.
A collection that includes the old generation; a full GC collects the whole heap. These are rarer and can pause for much longer than minor collections in stop-the-world designs.
Moving an object that has survived enough young collections into the old generation, also called tenuring.

A small piece of code the compiler or runtime runs alongside certain pointer stores, so the collector can keep its bookkeeping correct: recording old-to-young pointers for generational GC, or protecting concurrent marking.
example: Storing a new object into a field of an old cache object makes the write barrier mark that field's card dirty.

definition: A byte array in which each entry stands for a fixed-size 'card' of old-generation memory (512 bytes in a common HotSpot configuration). The write barrier marks a card dirty when a pointer is stored into it, so a minor GC scans only dirty cards.
example: A 20 GB old generation divided into 512-byte cards has about 40 million cards.

definition: A card-table entry marked by the write barrier because a pointer was stored somewhere in that card since the last collection; the next minor GC scans it for pointers into the young generation.
A record of the locations that hold pointers into a particular part of the heap (such as the young generation or a G1 region), so that part can be collected without scanning the whole heap.
A pause during which every application thread is halted so the collector can work on a heap that is not changing. Its length grows with the work done in it.
example: A full mark-compact of a 30 GB old generation can stop the world for seconds.

definition: A point in compiled code, such as a method call or loop back-edge, where the compiler has recorded which slots and registers hold pointers. Threads are brought to a safepoint before the collector examines their stacks.
The jump from the end of a loop body back to its start. Compilers often place safepoint checks there so long-running loops cannot delay a GC indefinitely.
HotSpot's simplest collector: single-threaded and stop-the-world for both young and old collections. Suited to small heaps and single-CPU machines.
HotSpot's throughput-oriented collector: it uses several GC threads, but all its collections are stop-the-world. Good for batch jobs where total run time matters more than pauses.
The free space between the live data and the heap's size or limit. More headroom means fewer collections and less GC work per allocated byte, at the cost of more memory.
example: A 3 GB heap holding 2 GB of live data has 1 GB of headroom.

definition: Using more memory to save computing time, or the reverse. Tracing GC is a classic case: a bigger heap means less collection work.
A state where the heap is so close to its live size that the collector runs almost continuously, consuming most of the CPU while freeing very little.
Garbage-collection jargon for the application code (its threads), which changes ('mutates') the object graph while the collector tries to trace it.
Memory a JVM program manages outside the garbage-collected heap (for example through ByteBuffer.allocateDirect), so the collector does not have to trace or move it.
How much memory a program actually uses. For a garbage-collected program it includes the live data plus the headroom the collector needs.
The value below which a given percentage of measurements fall. The p99 latency is the time that 99% of requests beat, so it shows the slowest 1%, where GC pauses appear.
example: If p99 is 105 ms, one request in a hundred takes longer than 105 ms.

definition: The latency of the slowest requests, measured by high percentiles such as p99 or p99.9. Rare GC pauses hardly move the average but dominate the tail.
Collection work that runs at the same time as the application's threads, rather than while they are stopped. It shortens pauses but needs barriers and costs extra CPU and memory headroom.
Collection work split across several GC threads at once, whether the application is stopped or not. Parallel and concurrent are independent properties.

Garbage-First, HotSpot's default collector since JDK 9. It divides the heap into equal regions, marks concurrently, and evacuates the regions with the most garbage first, trying to meet a soft pause-time goal.

HotSpot's low-latency collector, which marks and relocates objects concurrently using coloured pointers and load barriers, aiming for pauses that do not grow with heap size. Generational ZGC arrived in JDK 21 and became the only mode in JDK 24.
example: Enable it with `java -XX:+UseZGC`.

definition: A low-pause OpenJDK collector, originally developed by Red Hat, that compacts the heap concurrently with the application.

A way of describing marking progress: white objects have not been reached, grey ones have been reached but not scanned, and black ones have been reached and scanned. Marking ends when no grey objects remain; whatever is still white is garbage.
In tri-colour marking, an object the collector has not reached yet. At the end of marking, white objects are garbage.
In tri-colour marking, an object the collector has reached but whose fields it has not scanned yet; the grey objects are its work list.
In tri-colour marking, an object that has been reached and whose fields have all been scanned; the collector will not look at it again in this cycle.

The rule that concurrent marking must preserve to stay correct. The strong form says no black object may point at a white one; a weaker form allows it if the white object is still reachable through a grey object.

The concurrent-marking bug where the program stores a pointer to a white object into a black one and removes every grey path to it, so the collector never finds it and frees it while it is still in use. Barriers prevent it.
A write barrier (proposed by Dijkstra and colleagues) that shades the new target of a pointer store grey, so a black object can never be left pointing at a white one.
A write barrier (proposed by Yuasa) that shades the old target of an overwritten pointer grey, so nothing that was reachable when marking began can be lost. It is the basis of SATB.

Snapshot-at-the-beginning: a concurrent-marking approach, using a deletion barrier, that treats every object reachable when marking started as live. G1 and Shenandoah use it; objects that die during marking survive until the next cycle.
Objects that became unreachable during a concurrent collection cycle but are kept anyway because the collector treated them as live; they are freed in the next cycle.
Go's write barrier since Go 1.8, combining an insertion barrier and a deletion barrier, which removed the need to rescan goroutine stacks in a stop-the-world pause.
One of the many equal-sized blocks (often 1 to 32 MB) that G1 divides the heap into; each region currently plays one role, such as eden, survivor, old or humongous.
In G1, an object of half a region or more. It is allocated in its own run of contiguous regions, and many of them can cause fragmentation or early full GCs.
example: With 4 MB regions, a 3 MB array is humongous.

definition: A G1 collection that evacuates the young regions plus some old regions, chosen from those with the most garbage, after concurrent marking has measured each region's live data.
Copying the live objects out of a set of heap regions (the collection set) so those regions can be freed whole. G1 evacuates in stop-the-world pauses; ZGC relocates concurrently.
In G1, the heap occupancy (the initiating heap occupancy percent, IHOP) at which concurrent marking of the old generation starts. G1 adjusts it adaptively by default.
The target maximum pause a collector tries to meet, such as G1's -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis (default 200 ms). It is a soft goal that steers sizing decisions, not a guarantee.
The HotSpot JVM's automatic choice of settings, such as heap size, region size and collector, based on the machine it runs on.
JDK Enhancement Proposal: a numbered design document for a change to the JDK, such as JEP 439 (Generational ZGC).

ZGC's technique of keeping a few metadata bits inside each 64-bit object reference, recording which GC phase the pointer is valid ('good') for, so a load barrier can tell instantly whether it needs fixing.
A short check that runs when the program loads a reference from the heap. ZGC uses it to detect and repair pointers to objects that have been, or are being, relocated.
A barrier whose slow path writes the corrected pointer back into the field it loaded from, so later loads of that field take the fast path.
In a concurrent collector, a thread having to wait for memory because it allocates faster than the collector frees it; in effect, a pause.
The JVM option setting the maximum heap size.
example: `-Xmx64g` lets the heap grow to 64 GiB.

definition: The JVM option that selects ZGC as the garbage collector.
A record a runtime writes of each collection: when it ran, how long it paused and how much memory it freed. Enabled in Java with -Xlog:gc* and in Go with GODEBUG=gctrace=1.
A garbage collector that never relocates objects, so their addresses stay fixed. Go's collector is non-moving, which keeps interior pointers and calls into C simple, but cannot defragment the heap.
A collector that does not split the heap by object age, so every cycle traces all live data. Go's collector is non-generational.
A pointer to a field or element inside an object rather than to its start. Go allows them, which a non-moving collector handles easily.
example: In Go, `&s.field` is an interior pointer into s.

definition: Go's mechanism for calling C code from Go and Go from C.

The Go setting for how many OS threads may execute Go code at the same time. By default it is the number of logical CPUs the process may use; since Go 1.25 the default on Linux is also capped by a container's cgroup CPU limit. The GC aims to use 25% of it for background marking.
example: On an 8-core machine with no CPU limit, GOMAXPROCS is 8, so background marking aims for about 2 CPUs.

definition: In Go's collector, marking work a goroutine is made to do itself when it allocates during a GC cycle, so allocation cannot outrun marking.
The part of Go's runtime that decides when to start a GC cycle, aiming to finish marking just as the heap reaches its goal.

The main Go GC setting: the percentage the heap may grow past the live heap (plus roots) before the next cycle should finish. Default 100, which roughly doubles the live heap; GOGC=off disables growth-triggered collection.
example: With 400 MB live and GOGC=100 the heap goal is 800 MB.

definition: A Go setting (since Go 1.19) giving a soft limit on the total memory the Go runtime manages; as memory approaches it the GC runs more often, whatever GOGC says.
A memory limit the runtime tries to stay under by collecting more often, but may exceed rather than fail. Go's GOMEMLIMIT is one.
The heap size the Go GC aims to finish a cycle at, set by GOGC (and capped by GOMEMLIMIT). Ignoring roots it is the live heap × (1 + GOGC / 100).
example: 400 MB live at GOGC=100 gives an 800 MB heap goal.

definition: A failure mode where live data nears the memory limit, so the GC runs almost continuously and the program makes little progress. Go caps GC CPU at about 50% under the memory limit to soften it.
The Go function that runs a full garbage collection immediately and blocks until it finishes.
A request that is split into many parallel calls to backends and has to wait for all (or most) of them; a rare slow response on any one backend becomes common for the whole request.
Service-level objective: a target for a service's behaviour, such as 'p99 latency under 50 ms'.
A small, independently deployed service that does one job and talks to others over the network; one user request can fan out across many of them.
A Go standard-library cache of temporary objects that can be reused instead of allocated afresh, reducing GC work; the pool may drop its contents at any collection.
A program that processes a large amount of data with nobody waiting on individual responses, so total run time (throughput) matters more than pauses.
The region of source code where a variable exists, usually the block between braces. In Rust and C++ a value's destructor runs when its owning variable goes out of scope.
The Rust compiler error code for use of a value after it has been moved ("borrow of moved value"). Each code has a full explanation in the Rust error index.
The Rust compiler error code for two mutable borrows of the same value at the same time. Each code has a full explanation in the Rust error index.
The Rust compiler error code for a mutable borrow while a shared borrow of the same value is still in use (or the reverse). Each code has a full explanation in the Rust error index.
The Rust compiler error code for moving a value out while it is still borrowed. Each code has a full explanation in the Rust error index.
The Rust compiler error code for a borrowed value that does not live long enough for the reference to it. Each code has a full explanation in the Rust error index.

Rust's trait for explicit duplication: calling .clone() runs type-specific code. String clones its buffer, while Rc and Arc clones just add an owner of the same allocation, so clone is not always a deep copy.
example: `let b = a.clone();` gives b its own copy of a String's text.

definition: A copy that duplicates an object and everything it owns; a shallow copy duplicates only the top-level value, so the two share whatever it points to.
example: A Rust move copies a String's pointer, length and capacity (shallow); clone copies the text too (deep).

definition: Taking a reference to a value without taking ownership of it. A shared borrow (&T) allows reading and many may coexist; a mutable borrow (&mut T) allows writing and must be the only borrow in use.
example: `len(&s)` borrows s; s is still owned by the caller afterwards.

definition: A Rust reference that allows reading but (apart from interior-mutability types) not changing the value; any number can exist at once.
The core rule of Rust borrowing: at any moment a value may have many readers (shared references) or one writer (a mutable reference), never both. It rules out iterator invalidation and data races.
Exclusive or: true when exactly one of two conditions holds, not both.
A bug where a reference or iterator into a collection is used after the collection was changed in a way that moved or freed its elements, such as a push that reallocated a vector's buffer.
Moving a growable buffer to a new, bigger block of memory and freeing the old one, which invalidates any pointer into the old block.
example: A Vec with capacity 4 reallocates on its fifth push, typically to capacity 8.

definition: The Rust borrow checker's ability (stable since the 2018 edition) to end a borrow after its last use rather than at the end of its enclosing block, which removed many needless errors.
A versioned set of Rust language changes (2015, 2018, 2021, 2024) that a crate opts into, letting the language evolve without breaking old code.
A compile-time name, written like 'a, for the region of code in which a reference is valid. The borrow checker uses lifetimes to prove no reference outlives its value; they generate no machine code.
example: `fn longest<'a>(a: &'a str, b: &'a str) -> &'a str` says the result is valid only while both inputs are.

definition: Rust's rules for filling in lifetimes you leave out; for example, a function with exactly one reference parameter gives its returned reference that parameter's lifetime.
A Rust type that allows mutation through a shared reference by checking the borrowing rules at run time instead of compile time; a conflicting borrow_mut() panics. It is single-threaded only.
Rust's pattern of allowing a value to be changed through a shared (&) reference, using types such as Cell, RefCell and Mutex that enforce safety themselves.
Rust's mutual-exclusion lock that owns the data it protects: lock() returns a guard giving access, and the lock is released when the guard is dropped.
The value Rust's Mutex::lock() returns: it gives access to the protected data and unlocks the mutex automatically when it is dropped.
A C++ RAII class that locks a mutex when constructed and unlocks it in its destructor.
A Rust compiler lint, denied by default, that rejects `let _ = mutex.lock()`, because the wildcard drops the guard at once and the lock would be released immediately.
A value created while evaluating an expression and not stored in a named variable; it is normally destroyed at the end of the statement.
A safe Rust function that takes ownership of a value without running its destructor, deliberately leaking whatever it owns.
A safe Rust function that consumes a Box and returns a reference to its contents valid for the rest of the program, never freeing the memory.
In Rust, a pointer type (*const T or *mut T) with no borrow-checker guarantees; dereferencing it requires unsafe. In C and C++, any ordinary pointer, as opposed to a smart pointer.
Rust's marker traits for thread safety: a Send type may be moved to another thread, and a Sync type may be shared between threads by reference. Rc is neither, which is why it cannot cross threads.
The Rust compiler.
A widely used Rust graph library that stores nodes and edges in vectors and refers to them by index.
The official introductory book on Rust, known as 'the Book', free online.
Generating a separate compiled copy of generic code for each concrete type it is used with, as Rust and C++ do. It makes code fast but adds compile time.
The Java error thrown when a thread's stack runs out of room, typically because of very deep or unbounded recursion.
Short for 'no operation': a call or instruction that deliberately does nothing.
example: `free(NULL)` is a no-op in C.

definition: The property of code or data that it behaves correctly when used from several threads at the same time, usually through locks, atomic operations or immutability.
example: Rust's Arc is thread-safe; Rc is not, so the compiler forbids sharing it across threads.

definition: The library linked into every Go program that schedules goroutines, grows their stacks and runs the garbage collector.

In Rust, a panic raised while the program runs, for example when a RefCell is borrowed mutably while another borrow is active. It stops the thread in a defined way rather than causing undefined behaviour.
